title: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
description: Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. There are two other types of plague: bubonic
body: Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood. Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types.Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood.It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague. The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases. Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States.Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford.He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world."Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa. "Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact."Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas. You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal. But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact.You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs.It's thought that pneumonic plague was the main type of plague behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century.Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague. "I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said."Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form. "Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism. "This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks."According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours.If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal.But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early. Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health."Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease. "Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age. "It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early. "That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine."In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague. The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" – and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened.US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said there was "no indication of a broader threat to the United States".The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".

title: Jeffrey Archer: Queen Camilla pays tribute to 'irrepressible' author and former politician
description: Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novel
body: Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset.In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions.Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset and in 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth.He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman.He moved to the House of Lords in 1992 but was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001.He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages.The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker.The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi and producing fake diary entries to back up his story.He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial.He was released from jail in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news"."We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday.Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently."Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world."Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed – and long remembered".Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday.Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form."He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience."Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

schema.headline: Jeffrey Archer: Queen Camilla pays tribute to 'irrepressible' author and former politician

title: Kemi Badenoch: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK
description: Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next electio
body: Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election.The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another".Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories.As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions.Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different to the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election.She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles, external.Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them.She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win."The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority. "My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan."A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election. Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority."Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another".She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong".Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches.Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received, including a £5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong.Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down."That's what we're about."Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK.Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support.Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029.Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party".Elsewhere in her BBC interview, Badenoch said she was making changes to a policy for young people and was now proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) on earnings from 15% to 7.5% for those aged 21 to 24.The Tories announced last year that young people would see the first £5,000 of NI they would have paid in their first job redirected into a nominated savings account of their choice. The party said the policy, dubbed the "First Job Bonus", would have cost £2.8bn a year.On Tuesday, Badenoch said youth unemployed has "skyrocketed" and "you can't give people a first jobs bonus if they're not getting a first job".She added: "We're adapting and updating our policy so that it works for the problems they have today."The Conservatives said the new policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270.They added it "smooths the cliff edge" which exists as employer NI goes from 0% to the full rate when a worker turns 21.The government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities. Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training.Asked why the Conservatives were not proposing to cut NI for everyone, Badenoch said: "We have to find the money first. "So we have a golden economic rule. We are being fiscally credible. We find savings and then we spend it. "If I could afford to cut it for everybody, I promise you that I would. But young people have a much worse problem than everybody else."A Labour Party spokesperson said the NI announcement was "more fantasy economics from the Tories", adding the party had "allowed nearly one million of the next generation to be locked out of work or training".

schema.headline: Kemi Badenoch: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK

title: Why Tories are talking about winning the next election
description: Political party conferences can be weird events - where positive thinking and hopeful rhetoric can crowd out reality.If you spend enough time drinking
body: Political party conferences can be weird events - where positive thinking and hopeful rhetoric can crowd out reality.If you spend enough time drinking and socialising with like-minded people anything can seem possible.That could be one explanation for the upbeat mood of this year's Conservative gathering in Birmingham.On the face of it, the party has made little progress since it was emphatically ejected from power in 2024. If an election was held tomorrow, it would do even worse than it did back then, according to some polls.Yet senior figures, including leader Kemi Badenoch, are talking about winning the next general election outright and forming a government.One reason for their optimism is that they appear to have seen off, for now, the threat of being destroyed or swallowed up by Reform UK - a prospect which hung over last year's conference amid swirling rumours of defections and speculation about deals with Nigel Farage.Another is Badenoch herself, who appears to have made a positive impression on the public.Her approval rating has soared in recent months and she is now one of only two party leaders with a net positive rating (the other being Prime Minister Andy Burnham), according to pollsters More In Common., externalIn a presentation to a packed fringe meeting, More In Common's Luke Tryl said the Tory leader is seen as a "breath of fresh air" by focus groups, with many voters on the right describing her as someone unafraid to "say it as it is".In particular, her punchy performances at Prime Minister's Questions have made a strong impression, earning plaudits such as "intelligent", "professional" and "principled" from those who have seen her in action, according to Tryl.But like Burnham, Badenoch's personal popularity has yet to transfer to her party, he added, with the Tories being seen as "outdated" and "divided".It was not all gloom – in contrast to his presentation at last year's Tory conference –  and there were "signs of recovery", Tryl said, with a large pool of voters out there who might consider voting Tory, under the right circumstances.Conservatives freely admit the problem they have got is that voters don't trust them to deliver on any of their promises, when they had 14 years in government to do something about the problems they now say are so pressing."Of course, Kemi's ahead of us, we know that," Conservative chairman Kevin Hollinrake told the More in Common meeting."Because people do trust Kemi and they don't trust us, that's how I would put it in a nutshell."But we are building on that."Badenoch answers the trust question by saying that the party is under new management now.She has ditched some of the "culture war" rhetoric and is focusing hard on the economy, and setting out her guiding principles, which amount to a return to old-school Conservatism.She is not saying that the party could win an election outright if it was held now, arguing that no one could.But she has ruled out governing with Reform UK in a hung parliament, telling the BBC she would rather hold another election.Hollinrake sounded a cautious note at the More In Common fringe."We are not where we need to be right now. We don't want an election right now, ideally. Ideally, it would come way down the track."But deputy leader Alex Burghart was quick to stress that the party is making every effort to ensure it is ready for a snap election."We are preparing for an election now," he told the meeting."We are convinced we can win the election outright."He claimed the Tories were more united than at any time in their recent history, with the possible exception of the aftermath of Boris Johnson's 2019 victory.But they still trail Reform by four or five points in the polls and are as much as nine points behind Labour.The next challenge for the party, former Scottish Conservative leader Dame Ruth Davidson said, was to become one of the "top two".At that point, voters who want to see the back of Labour would start moving to the Tories in serious numbers, she argued.Tactical voting could prove crucial at the next election, whenever it comes, with many people voting to keep parties out of power rather than for who they want to win.The Tories think they have a strong hand here too."For the first time in history, the Conservative Party is now the least hated political party in the country," declared Hollinrake, to laughter and applause."When it comes to tactical voting, that's really important."Not the most inspiring rallying cry you will hear at a party conference, perhaps, but it is grounded in reality.

schema.headline: Why Tories are talking about winning the next election

title: Dread presenting at work? Read these tips before your next meeting
description: Image source, Studio Grey for Social Market FoundationImage caption, Dani Payne would have panic attacks at the thought of presenting - now she does i
body: Image source, Studio Grey for Social Market FoundationImage caption, Dani Payne would have panic attacks at the thought of presenting - now she does it most daysByEmily HoltUpdated 9 hours agoDani Payne was so anxious about public speaking, she had a doctor's note to excuse her from presenting at school and university.Now aged 28 with a job in politics at a cross-party think tank, she's spoken in parliament, sits on discussion panels and presents social media videos. "Most days I do some form of public speaking," she says. "I wouldn't have believed that at 15."Want to get better, or simply get started? Here are four ways to help you nail your presentation or speech.Woman's HourSpeaking in Public: Why it feels so hard to do and how to do it anyway. Listen now.1. Start with your passionPayne, from Exeter, says she stopped any form of public speaking after developing a severe anxiety disorder and experiencing panic attacks.But looking back, she says avoiding it didn't help her build "coping skills or resilience". "The more you avoid what you're anxious about, the more you're anxious about it."In her second year of university she was invited to present a subject she was passionate about. "I realised I was losing out on opportunities that I felt really strongly about."She presented research for her dissertation on sexual misconduct in academic fieldwork settings and that was the start of conquering her fear.Her advice is to look for or create opportunities to speak about something you care about. "Picking something you genuinely feel passionately about will always make it easier," she says. 2. Practise in virtual realityImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A virtual reality headset can help you present in front of a pretend audienceDaisy Schofield, a 32-year-old documentary producer and journalist, had her first panic attack at university during a presentation, she tells Woman's Hour.She managed to avoid public speaking until she got her first job and had to present company statistics on Teams every Monday. To build her confidence, Schofield practises by using an app on her phone to create a fake audience in a virtual reality headset she bought online for £10. "It makes practising feel much more engaging and like the real thing, compared to practising at home on your own, which feels a bit awkward and boring."3. Choose one wordImage source, Fred Ferschke for EmotionImage caption, Stand-up comedian Viv GroskopViv Groskop,  a stand-up comedian, writer and public speaking coach advises picking a word that encapsulates what you want your speech to convey. "It could be something like clarity... you can think to yourself afterwards, 'did I set out to be clear? Was I clear? Yes. It's a win.' And every time you choose a different word."Groskop also advises putting a post-it note on your laptop camera and reminding yourself to look there and not at people on the screen "because it will mean you're looking down, not at people."When you're presenting in person, Prof Nazanin Derakhshan, a neuroscientist at Birkbeck, University of London, advises not to focus too much on people's faces."Accept that their facial expression may mean anything, and distract yourself internally from interpreting these facial expressions."4. Expect mistakesPayne says being good at public speaking does not come "naturally to someone"."You wouldn't pick up a guitar, and be surprised that you couldn't play a song when you've never picked up a guitar before - public speaking is the exact same thing."Groksop says people who are good at public speaking have just been doing it more."Many people are spending up to eight hours a day on Teams or Zoom, and if you think about a television newsreader, they've been trained for that."She says no one around you expects you to "immediately be a master public speaker the first time you do it".Derakhshan says being vulnerable is a "big asset" when public speaking. "We all make mistakes, we all forget things. It's not the end of the world. If you can go back and make a humour of it the audience are quite forgiving and accepting."Additional Reporting by Simon Richardson.

title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
description: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The ta
body: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers. It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network. Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings to add to its existing catalogue of hit franchises which includes Indiana Jones, Mission: Impossible and Shrek. The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover. Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry."From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said.Asked about the merger after it had been finalised, US President Donald Trump described the deal as "great"."They're terrific people and it's going to be a great company," he said.Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive.Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the  newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology.Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News.Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation". "While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned.Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said the company has high debts at a time when interest rates are high."The combined entity, now called Skydance, needs to cut costs and make bigger profits to be able to get the debt down to more manageable levels," he said."The fact Tom Cruise movie Digger, Warner Bros' last release before the merger, has been a major flop is a reminder of how the film industry is not a guaranteed ticket to riches."While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning.Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away. Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide". US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead.As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS.Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount.Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained.Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons.Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours. The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick. The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement. To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films.As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob.Paramount also must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising to more than 30% through the following three years.

schema.headline: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger

title: We're saving £100 a month for our kids but they won't get it until they're 57
description: Image source, Richard BrainImage caption, Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices nowByElizab
body: Image source, Richard BrainImage caption, Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices nowByElizabeth AndersonBusiness reporterUpdated 09:16 BSTRichard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them.The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules., externalSo the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083.Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing."Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow."'We don't eat out as often as we used to'Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council.He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended.In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18.The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life.Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past."We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain."And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids."'I want to retire earlier so this will help'Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600.The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show. One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open, external as in the same period a year earlier. Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023.While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more?Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years."The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help."Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says.Image source, Hugo ThompsonImage caption, Hugo Thompson is happy to wait until he is at least 57 to access the pension fundFor parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity."Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound."It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children.In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts.Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half.Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three.Image source, Wally LuckeydooImage caption, Wally Luckeydoo says he is giving his children a "financial head start""My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally."For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt."I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

title: Paramount-Warner Bros merger: Four ways the deal could affect you
description: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect youImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paramount and Warner Bros are comin
body: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect youImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form SkydanceByFrancisco VelasquezBusiness reporterReporting fromNew York and Regan MorrisReporting fromCaliforniaUpdated 1 hour agoIt has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.  Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.1. Streaming prices may riseImage source, Eddy Chen/HBOImage caption, HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring ZendayaWarner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS. Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time. While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come. While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes". 2. More film releasesImage source, Getty ImagesAs part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years. For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas. The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein. Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date."Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said."Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".  Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema. As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas. Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year. 3. Hollywood jobs could be hitImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LAFor those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground. Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods. Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken". "It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment,  it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years. The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities". She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts. "Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added. 4. CNN and CBS could changeImage source, ReutersImage caption,  CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the buildingTo address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount. The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN. Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation. Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role. Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS. Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.  Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless"."The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said. Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said. schema.headline: Paramount-Warner Bros merger: Four ways the deal could affect you

title: 'ASOS hacked': App users receive notifications sent by hackers
description: Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sen
body: Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers. Dozens of people told the BBC they received the strange "ASOS HACKED" message from the clothing and beauty store's app on Tuesday morning - with some saying it left them "scared" to open the app.The notification was addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams in what cyber security experts said looked like a "brazen" extortion attempt.Asos acknowledged the "unauthorised customer notification" on Tuesday afternoon, saying some "basic personal information" may have been accessed.In an email to customers on Tuesday night, the company apologised and urged customers not to engage with the notification. And it said the website and app are "operating as usual" promising customers they can "shop with confidence" while it investigates the incident. The company has not as of yet informed the UK's data watchdog, the Information Commission's Office (ICO), about any breach.Exactly how many Asos customers received the notification on Tuesday remains unclear, but Google's Play store says the ASOS app has been downloaded to android devices more than 10 million times. The British retailer has a substantial global footprint - serving around 17 million customers each year across more than 150 markets.Some Asos app users in Australia, France, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland had also received the notification, according to local reports on Tuesday.Hackers seeking to pile pressure on potential victims by informing their customers is rare, as most extortions happen in private, so this incident may go down as a significant moment in cyber-attack history.Shares in the company fell by around a tenth on Tuesday. Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, called it a "deeply serious" and "brazen" attack whereby the hackers had apparently "turned Asos' own app into their ransom note".But she told the BBC that Asos customers should not be "scared and frightened" - encouraging those worried to change their passwords, avoid clicking on the notification's link and be cautious about possible scam emails or texts."My main concern is that my information, such as bank information, home address, telephone number, has been compromised," said Erin, a student at the University of Sheffield.She told the BBC that while her friends have expressed similar concerns about a potential data leak, her sister did not receive the notification on the Asos app."So the question is what is the extent? Are all customers affected even if they didn't get the notification? It's poor from Asos on all fronts."Asos said in its statement that it took "immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms" on Tuesday - adding it was working with specialists within and outside the company, as well as relevant authorities.It said it does not believe payment-card information or account passwords were impacted, and that its site and app are "operating as normal"."Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate," it said.The BBC understands the National Cyber Security Centre has offered assistance to Asos.Meanwhile Snowflake - whose tools are used by dozens of firms to collect, analyse and store data - told the BBC its investigation was ongoing, but it had so far found "no compromise" of its platform.The company's services have, however, been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years.

schema.headline: 'ASOS hacked': App users receive notifications sent by hackers

title: Worcestershire student admits murdering woman in 'Dexter' kill room
description: Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressingA forensic science student obsessed with the US television drama Dexter has ad
body: Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressingA forensic science student obsessed with the US television drama Dexter has admitted murdering a 24-year-old woman after luring her to a plastic-lined "kill room" inside an Airbnb.Benjamin William Day, 20, changed his plea to guilty on the second day of his trial at Wolverhampton Crown Court.Prosecutors said he had carefully planned the killing of Maria Saceanu on 20 December, preparing a room with plastic sheeting and items intended to help him murder her and dispose of evidence.Day, who was 19 when the murder took place, was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced on 4 December.The University of Worcester undergraduate, of Yeadon Close in Redditch, Worcestershire, had been expected to argue he acted in self-defence and had set up the room to film a Dexter tribute for TikTok.But after an hour-long delay to proceedings earlier, Day returned to the dock and appeared to smirk as he entered a guilty plea.Prosecutor Rachel Brand KC said he had been fascinated by the programme Dexter, which centres on a forensic scientist in a police department who knows how to cover his own tracks as a serial killer.Day had set up the the rented room in the Tividale area of the West Midlands to emulate the character - lining the walls and floor with plastic sheeting to cover his tracks and amassing a "shopping list" of items, including an apron, a plastic visor and cleaning chemicals. The first day of the trial heard that after causing 78 knife wounds to sex worker Saceanu, who he contacted through a website using a burner phone, Day abandoned the "gruesome task" of dismemberment because he cut himself.Prosecutors claim Day left the Airbnb after the killing, walked some distance away, and called 999 at 00:50 on 21 December asking for medical help.On body cam footage played to jurors on Tuesday, Day could be seen sitting in a police car with his hand wrapped in duct tape.He said he had been going to drink in Dudley and had been looking for a "random girl" in a bar when he claimed he had been injured near a bush by an animal that "might have been a fox". Questioned as to where he had got duct tape to wrap around his hand, Day told police it was in his car, although he could not remember where it was parked.A male officer told him that his story did not quite check out, to which Day responded: "I don't know if it was a wild dog or a fox."Police were alerted to the scene at the Airbnb by the property's landlord, who had been contacted by another resident who had booked into a different room and had discovered a trail of blood. In a statement the resident told jurors they had pushed open the door and saw "a lot of blood on the floor" and what appeared to be a doll. "The doll was lying on the floor on its back," they added. When Day was arrested on suspicion of murder at Russells Hall Hospital in Dudley in the early hours of the morning of 21 December he was wearing a khaki top resembling one worn by Dexter.A Home Office pathologist said Saceanu, originally from Romania, probably died as a result or wounds to her neck, causing damage to her carotid arteries, with a number of wounds to her hands "consistent with efforts to protect herself".Defence barrister Gurdeep Garcha KC said of Day: "He is well aware of the nature and inevitability of the sentence that must follow."It seems to us that given his age and the absence of (previous) criminal offending, the court would be assisted by a pre-sentence report."

schema.headline: Worcestershire student admits murdering woman in 'Dexter' kill room

title: Small inflatable boats 'set for people smugglers' seized at East Midlands Airport
description: Minister for border security and asylum Anna Turley added: "This seizure of 25 small boats delivers yet another blow to the evil smuggling gangs."Disr
body: Minister for border security and asylum Anna Turley added: "This seizure of 25 small boats delivers yet another blow to the evil smuggling gangs."Disruptions to supply lines like these are happening more than ever before as we bear down on the illegal and dangerous crossings."The NCA said about 100 investigations into gangs involved in organisation immigration crime were ongoing.Adam Berry, branch commander for the alternative disruption team, confirmed it was the first time it had made a seizure of air freight in the UK."These boats are so dangerous," he said. "We have sadly seen so many deaths in the Channel recently, and it's because they are just purely constructed to get across as cheaply and as flimsily as possible."What we can see when we get the boats and we blow the boats up is that there's distinctive shapes and types of them."There's a distinctive transom - which is the bit where the engine sits - and then you've got how many chambers they are, the construction of them and other key bits."We can look at boats that have arrived and we can compare them to these and prove that these boats are the exact boats that we have seen in the Channel."

schema.headline: Small inflatable boats 'set for people smugglers' seized at East Midlands Airport

title: China Open: Daniil Medvedev finally runs out of chances with disqualification against Novak Djokovic
description: Daniil Medvedev once said you would need to knock on his hotel door at 6am for seven days in a row to make him angry.On court, though, he is a far mor
body: Daniil Medvedev once said you would need to knock on his hotel door at 6am for seven days in a row to make him angry.On court, though, he is a far more combustible character who finally ran out of chances when he was disqualified from Monday's China Open semi-final against Novak Djokovic.Djokovic was serving for a place in the final when the ball ricocheted off the back of the court. Medvedev swiped it into the stands, where it hit a spectator in the face.A few minutes later the Russian was defaulted, as he had to be, under rules that bar a player from "hitting a ball dangerously or recklessly, or with negligent disregard of the consequences."Players have got away with worse. There is sometimes anger in their actions, but it is rarely of the bulging-neck-vein variety.It is more often a sign of irritation and petulance, with frustrations taken out on the ball with little care for the safety of officials, ball kids and the spectators who line the court."I can only say I'm a really calm person in life - I actually have no idea why the demons go out when I play tennis," Medvedev said at the 2019 US Open, where he was fined for snatching a towel from a ball person and making an offensive gesture to fans inside the Arthur Ashe Stadium."Especially when I was a junior, I had a lot of problems with my attitude."I was not getting defaulted, but to have a game penalty was easy."Returning to the theme at that year's end-of-season ATP Finals, Medvedev said any bad blood soon disappears after leaving the court."All my temper goes away after I leave the tennis court. If I'm not happy with my practice, I step out of the court and five minutes later, I'm OK," he said.It is hard - and probably unwise - to take your eyes off Medvedev's matches, and he is very popular with the media for his engaging, reflective and humorous interviews once the dust has settled.But he has gone too far on court on many occasions, with much of his aggression directed at umpires.At Wimbledon in 2017, a 21-year-old Medvedev was so incensed about some of the decisions made by umpire Mariana Alves in his second-round match that he sprinkled coins at her feet as she climbed down from the chair.He later apologised and denied he was accusing her of bias.Two years ago, again at Wimbledon, it appeared officials were considering defaulting Medvedev for an outburst towards umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore.Medvedev claimed he said something in Russian which was "not pleasant, but not over the line" - and, after a discussion between the umpire, supervisor and tournament referee, he escaped with a code violation for unsportsmanlike conduct.He was fined more than £60,000 for his behaviour at the 2025 Australian Open, which included trying to destroy a net camera, and had an infamous meltdown later that year at the US Open.On a rowdy New York night, Benjamin Bonzi had match point for a straight-set win against Medvedev in the first round when a photographer inexplicably walked on to court between his first and second serves.Umpire Greg Allensworth awarded the Frenchman another first serve because of the delay, sparking fury from Medvedev.Medvedev accused Allensworth of hoping to engineer a quick finish - as he gets paid by the match, rather than the hour - and there was a pause of over five minutes as he whipped up the crowd.He did save the match point, but went on to lose in five sets before obliterating his racquet by smashing it repeatedly against the table next to his chair.

schema.headline: China Open: Daniil Medvedev finally runs out of chances with disqualification against Novak Djokovic

title: Cristiano Ronaldo: Portugal forward not retiring but says he wants to be punished for 'breach of coach's trust'
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after he committed a "br
body: Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after he committed a "breach of the coach's trust".The 41-year-old captain left his country's Nations League camp after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.In a lengthy statement, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player said he should be held accountable for his actions."The Portuguese Football Federation must assess the consequences of my actions and punish me for them. I believe the punishment should not be reduced," Ronaldo said."I have already apologised, but I know that actions have consequences."Portugal manager Jorge Jesus said on Sunday that the door was still open for Ronaldo to play for the country's national team.Ronaldo said that, provided he was "physically fit, playing with my team, and hopefully scoring goals", he would like to continue to play international football."After my suspension period ends, I will be available, as I always have been, to compete and win with our national team," he added.Ronaldo's statement, which ran to nearly 2,000 words, struck a conciliatory tone in places but was also critical of Portugal coach Jesus as he provided his version of the dispute which prompted him to walk out on the squad last week.He said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the 72-year-old coach told him he would play for 30 minutes."Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said."The manager had broken his word to me."A later meeting with Jesus produced an agreement for the coach to clarify matters at his next news conference.Ronaldo said an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus' decisions and that the coach asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake.Portugal'a all-time appearance holder said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach's public remarks did not reflect their private discussion."It was the second time he had broken his word to me," Ronaldo explained. "I decided to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises."More to follow.

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo: Portugal forward not retiring but says he wants to be punished for 'breach of coach's trust'

title: Men jailed for raping teenage girl after grooming her on Snapchat
description: Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Awal Ahmadzai, Salman Habibkheil and Mehrab Safi fled the UK after committing a string of sexual
body: Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Awal Ahmadzai, Salman Habibkheil and Mehrab Safi fled the UK after committing a string of sexual offences against a 17-year-old girlByCheryl DennisReporting fromBristol Crown Court and Leigh BoobyerBristolUpdated 3 hours agoThree Afghan nationals who raped a teenager, before being stopped by French police as they fled the UK in the back of a lorry, have been jailed.Mehrab Safi, 21, Awal Ahmadzai and Salman Habibkheli, both 19, were found guilty on 26 June of multiple offences against the girl at a house in St Werburghs, Bristol, last year.Safi first met the 17-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, while she was Christmas shopping, and groomed her over Snapchat before paying for a taxi to bring her to Bristol.Safi was jailed for 15 years at Bristol Crown Court on Tuesday, while Habibkheli and Ahmadzai were both sentenced to nine years in a youth detention centre.Sentencing the three men, Judge Michael Cullum said being trafficked and raped by the men will have caused "unimaginable" trauma to the teenager.Warning: This story contains distressing details.Figure caption, Footage of rapists fleeing UK in back of lorryA 17-year-old boy - who is an Afghan national but cannot be named for legal reasons - was also convicted of rape, but he did not try to escape the UK. He was sentenced to two years and seven months in a youth detention centre. In a victim impact statement read out to the court, the girl said the attack had left her "traumatised" and fearful of leaving the house.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Safi transported the girl by taxi from Somerset to a house in Bristol where she was raped by the men and boyShe added that she is a "different person" to who she was a year ago."I had a lot more friends, I would go out a lot more, I was happier. Now, I've stopped going out, I don't even leave the house in general. "If I ever leave the house, it is only with my best friend or mum. I would not be able to go out by myself, even the thought of that makes me panic."Generally my brain keeps blocking out the trauma that happened to me, but when I am feeling low emotionally it all comes back and makes me feel even worse."Sometimes I would dream about what happened, which I was not expecting – and I do not like those dreams at all," she said.Image caption, Det Sgt Jo Babbage praised the bravery of the victim for reporting the attacksAvon and Somerset Police said the girl, who was from Somerset, was plied with alcohol when she arrived at Safi's home. She was then sexually assaulted and raped over a number of hours by the three men and teenager in November last year.Officers attended the property and found the girl after her mother reported her missing. Det Sgt Jo Babbage said the victim had begun communicating with Safi five days before the attacks "via mobile, predominantly Snapchat". She said: "It's clear that that's where the grooming and the contact process was started that led up to her being brought into Bristol by taxi which was arranged [by Safi]."Babbage said the girl has been left "very traumatised" by the attacks, but has been "very brave" throughout the investigation. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The victim met one of the men while she was Christmas shopping at the Cabot Circus shopping centre in BristolThe victim came to Bristol for the first time on 25 November 2025 with a friend on a Christmas shopping trip.During the trip, the girl met Safi and they exchanged numbers and Snapchat contacts.Safi later used the platform to persuade her to send nude photos.He then arranged for a taxi to take her from her home to his house in St Werburghs in the early hours of 30 November where he and the three others carried out the attacks.Babbage said: "Just hearing that, reading it, this Christmas shopping trip that ended like that, as a parent, makes you feel terrified for your children to go out."Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, The court heard the victim was plied with alcohol when she arrived at the houseThe 17-year-old boy was arrested at the scene, but the three men fled from officers and travelled to Birmingham and London before they left the country in a lorry.They were discovered by French police in Calais and returned to the UK where they were immediately arrested on suspicion of rape.Babbage said: "They got into the back of a lorry... and they were able to leave the country without documents and it was just fortuitous that our friends in France located them and were able to return them straight away." Mobile phone footage from Safi's phone showed the men laughing and gesticulating in the back of the lorry, which the prosecution said during the trial had suggested they thought they had "got away with it".'Unimaginable' traumaSentencing the men and teenager, Judge Cullum said the victim would have looked "vulnerable from the very beginning". "I have no doubt that was her attraction to you, Safi. After an intense exchange of texts you obtained nude photos of her. "Reading of the exchanges is uncomfortable and starts to suggest an imbalance of power between you [Safi] and the victim. "Having been trafficked she was raped five times, and cumulative trauma will undoubtedly live with her forever and is unimaginable," he said.During sentencing, the judge acknowledged the traumatic experiences all four had endured in Afghanistan. The judge also noted that one of them had lost a parent at the hands of the Taliban.However, he said that this was no excuse.All four were also sentenced to be put on the sex offender's register indefinitely, and received a sexual harm prevention order which stops them communicating with children.Get in touchYour Voice
